children: , the processor-architecture licensor, turned Muse's early traction into another powerful AI-compute trade Monday. American depositary shares surged approximately 11.6% to $307.64, extending the market's bet that persistent AI agents could drive far more computing activity than today's chatbot-style workloads. The valuation picture is already aggressive: the shares now sit 58.66% above the $193.90 GF Value estimate, suggesting investors are pricing in substantial future growth.

Barron's cited Arm's estimate that the server-CPU market could reach $120 billion by 2030, with annual growth above 35%. Muse adds another potential demand engine. Unlike a simple AI query that ends when the answer appears, persistent agents can keep browsing, coordinating tasks, handling security checks and running workflows in the background. More autonomous activity means more CPU work sitting around the AI model itself exactly the kind of expanding infrastructure footprint that could enlarge Arm's royalty opportunity.

The catch is attribution. Arm makes money through licensing and royalties tied to partner designs and shipment volumes, so a larger compute market does not automatically translate into Arm revenue. Muse has not disclosed which CPU architecture or infrastructure suppliers power its workloads, leaving the direct connection unproven for now. Investors are therefore paying for a broader thesis: if autonomous agents multiply server workloads and Arm keeps gaining content across data-center designs, royalty growth could follow. At $307.64, however, the stock is already demanding that a meaningful portion of that thesis becomes real.

title: Arm Rises 8.8% as Muse Expands AI's CPU Royalty Funnel
